span: Their plea was of adverse possession against the appellant, which presupposes that the appellant was the owner.
why: Court treats a defendant's plea of perfected title by adverse possession as a procedural point about the maintainability of an injunction suit; it neither affirms nor denies that title can be acquired.

span: but also to vest the possessor with title
why: Headnote states that limitation statutes vest the possessor with title, which supports the proposition; the same headnote stresses strict pleading and proof, and headnote confidence is capped.

span: To establish a claim of title by prescription, that is, adverse possession for 12 years or more, the possession of the claimant must be physical/actual, exclusive, open, uninterrupted, notorious and hostile
why: Court recognises title by prescription but states strict conditions and that permissive possession does not qualify; no application to a claimant's success in this passage.

span: his right is forever extinguished and the possessory owner acquires an absolute title
why: Perry v. Clissold is quoted as the definition of the principle; the court introduces it as a definition and goes on to list requirements, but its own holding on the Government land comes later.

span: Mere possession of the land would not ripen into possessory title.
why: A High Court judge's earlier statement of the prerequisites of adverse possession is quoted; the passage does not apply it or state the court's own view on the proposition.

span: observed that title can be based on adverse possession
why: The court reports an earlier decision as saying title can be based on adverse possession and also that the law is harsh; the current court's adoption is suggested by its later discussion but is not shown here.
